title: Power torsion depends only on the closed subset: a module is I-power torsion exactly when its support lies in V(I)

standard_prerequisites.name: An element of a module that maps to zero in the localization at f is annihilated by a power of f, and vanishing of the localizations at every prime not containing I is equivalent to vanishing of the localizations at the elements f of I when I is finitely generated
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: used at proof lines 24095-24100, where the passage from localizations at primes to localizations at the generators f_1, ..., f_r of I is made
standard_prerequisites.use: Converts the support condition into explicit annihilation by the generators of I.

standard_prerequisites.name: The support of an R-module is the set of primes at which its localization is nonzero, and V(I) is the set of primes containing I
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: used throughout statement and proof, notably at proof line 24097 and at the description of the kernel at proof lines 24101-24102
standard_prerequisites.use: Provides the vocabulary in which both the hypothesis and the conclusion of the lemma are stated.

standard_prerequisites.name: The submodule of elements annihilated by a power of I is the kernel of the map to the product of the localizations at the primes outside V(I)
standard_prerequisites.use: Turns the elementwise equivalence into an identification of the I-power torsion submodule, from which both assertions follow.

core_obligations: Take an R-module M and an element x of M, and prove the forward implication: if x is annihilated by a power of I, then x maps to zero in the localization M_f for every f in I, hence in M_p for every prime p not containing I (proof lines 24095-24097).
Prove the converse elementwise: if x maps to zero in M_p for all primes p with I not contained in p, then x maps to zero in M_f for every f in I (proof lines 24097-24099).

Use the finite generation I = (f_1, ..., f_r) to extract exponents: from the vanishing of the images in the M_{f_i} obtain integers n_i at least 1 with f_i^{n_i} x = 0, and conclude that x is annihilated by I to the power sum of the n_i, which makes x an element of the I-power torsion submodule (proof lines 24099-24101).

Identify the power torsion submodule M[I^infinity] with the kernel of the map M -> product over primes outside V(I) of M_p, deduce the characterisation by support, and conclude that the subcategory of I-power torsion modules depends only on the closed subset V(I) (proof lines 24101-24104).
proof_roadmap: Show that an element annihilated by a power of I dies in every localization at an element of I, and hence in every localization at a prime outside V(I) (proof lines 24095-24097).

Conversely, suppose an element dies in all those localizations; using that I is finitely generated, lift the vanishing to the localizations at the finitely many generators and read off the annihilating exponents (proof lines 24097-24100).

Express the power torsion submodule as the kernel of the map into the product of the localizations outside V(I), obtaining the support characterisation and the independence of the presentation of the closed set (proof lines 24101-24104).
difficulty_reason: The lemma states that for a ring R with a finitely generated ideal I, the subcategory of I-power torsion modules depends only on the closed subset Z = V(I) of Spec(R), and that a module is I-power torsion exactly when its support is contained in Z (statement lines 24085-24092). The proof is an elementwise computation that has to go through the localizations twice: an element annihilated by a power of I dies in the localizations at the elements of I and hence at the primes outside V(I), while conversely vanishing at all those primes must be lifted back to vanishing at the finitely many localizations M_{f_i}, which is where the finite generation of I is used, and only then do the annihilating exponents appear (proof lines 24095-24101). The last line identifies the power torsion submodule as the kernel of the map to the product of the localizations outside Z, and the dependence on the closed set rather than on the ideal follows from that description.
